sewer_sink.n: Sewer as heat source or sink
sewer_sink.f: Q = flow × 4.18 × ΔT, within the temperature rules: sewage arriving at the plant ≥ 11 °C when used as a source (KWL design rule); waste entering a facility < 40 °C, non-domestic waste < 65 °C when used as a sink (Bylaw 299)
sewer_sink.c: Vancouver: ~45 MW city-wide, ~100 MW region-wide (KWL 2014, secondary); NEU uses 3.2 + 6.6 MW; access first-come first-served with a letter of support (UT-008); heat user pays access costs; per-pipe flow near a parcel is not published (only North Surrey 6 MW). Edmonton: no EPCOR sewer-heat programme or data found; non-contact cooling water to sanitary sewer needs EWSI written approval (Bylaw 19627 Sch. 2 s. 5.10); Edmonton: Blatchford's planned sewer heat exchange centre (two combined sewers under the future market area) was deferred after EPCOR reduced its sewer-flow forecasts (Blatchford Budget and Plans 2023–2026) — the first Edmonton evidence on sewer heat, and a caution
sewer_sink.st: rules in hand for Vancouver; flow at a parcel and all Edmonton figures are gaps
sewer_sink.pl: Sewer as heat source or sink

surface_water_sink.n: Sea or river water as a cooling sink
surface_water_sink.f: capacity set by the thermal limit at the outfall and mixing, not by the licence: marine ±1 °C (BC, CCME), Burrard Inlet proposed "no further increase"; Alberta freshwater +3 °C over ambient
surface_water_sink.c: BC licence: cooling application $1,000; heat-exchange rental $2.25 per 1,000 m³ (min $200); DFO intake screens 2.54 mm, approach velocity 0.035–0.055 m/s (internal conflict — confirm); Alberta Water Act review as for any industrial project; Toronto Enwave precedent: 4 °C in, ≤13 °C out, 50-year agreement | 19 Oct 2026 (K): Burrard Inlet bottom water 7.6–13.9 °C all year (False Creek not sampled); North Saskatchewan near 0 °C in winter with frazil-ice risk, summer not found; flow 24–49 L/s per MW at a 10–5 °C rise (derived); pipe about US$2,120–2,150/m (Hawaii 2002, deep ocean, an upper bound); BC: cooling water needs a waste discharge authorization, Port category C for a new discharge (60–120 business days ?); Edmonton: river valley plan allows major facilities only where essential and bans utility corridors except crossings. Distance to shore not computed: no shoreline file in the tool yet | 19 Oct 2026 (K): Burrard Inlet bottom water 7.6–13.9 °C all year (False Creek not sampled); North Saskatchewan near 0 °C in winter with frazil-ice risk, summer not found; flow 24–49 L/s per MW at a 10–5 °C rise (derived); pipe about US$2,120–2,150/m (Hawaii 2002, deep ocean, an upper bound); BC: cooling water needs a waste discharge authorization, Port category C for a new discharge (60–120 business days ?); Edmonton: river valley plan allows major facilities only where essential and bans utility corridors except crossings. distance to the water: Edmonton from the North Saskatchewan …

self_gen_rules.n: Rules for generation beside the data centre
self_gen_rules.f: export cap and compensation by province; connection priority for paired generation (Alberta)
self_gen_rules.c: BC: RS 2289 from 1 Jul 2026, export up to 100 kW per phase (or ≤100 kW nameplate) at $0.10/kWh, same or adjacent parcel; RS 2289 applies only at distribution voltage, so a data centre supplied at 60 kV or higher (RS 1830) cannot use it; community generation up to 2 MW. Alberta: micro-generation ≤5 MW (retail credit <150 kW, wholesale above); data centres paired with dedicated new generation or storage go to the front of the connection line (Alta Reg 117/2026, government summary) | 19 Oct 2026 (L): BC Hydro describes RS 2289 as generation on your own property; the formal location clause (same or adjacent parcel) is not confirmed
self_gen_rules.pl: Rules for generating power on site

electricity_price.n: Price of power at the site
electricity_price.f: tariff for the customer class: BC Hydro LGS or Transmission (RS 1830); Alberta pool price + EPCOR (Edmonton) or FortisAlberta (Parkland) distribution and transmission
electricity_price.c: BC LGS (RS 1600–1611, effective 1 Apr 2026): $13.83/kW, 6.79 ¢/kWh, 29.99 ¢/day; RS 1830 (supply at 60 kV or higher, effective 1 Apr 2026): $12.178/kVA, 4.914 ¢/kWh; loads >150 MW pay full incremental cost; 300 MW AI + 100 MW DC allocation. Alberta: pool $43.68/MWh (2025), $62.78 (2024); EPCOR DAS-TOUP and SAS-TOUP; FortisAlberta Rate 63; Rate of Last Resort not available to these loads. Replaces the first attempt's assumed $80–120/MWh; BC's over-150 MW full-cost rule is stated for industrial customers on the North Coast line; data centres not named: context, not a rule for the Vancouver site [decision 30 Oct 2026] P-12 (30 Oct 2026): the BC Hydro demand charge is billed monthly, so a year is 12 × the monthly charge. Edmonton energy: pool $43.68 + EPCOR $2.50/MWh + 7.99% = $49.67/MWh (epcorDASSAS). The large general service rate applies at distribution voltage; transmission service (RS 1830, 60 kV or higher) is not applied; the size at which BC Hydro requires it is not sourced (?).
electricity_price.pl: Price of power at the site

water_supply.f: potable at the metered rate; reclaimed where a utility offers it to industry
water_supply.c: Vancouver 2026: water $4.091–5.128 per unit + sewer $7.960 per unit ? (unit = 2.832 m³), no large-user rate; Metro Vancouver reclaimed water case-by-case, no rate. Edmonton: EPCOR supplied 4,226 ML of reclaimed water to industry in 2024 (price, customers not stated); commercial potable rates not extracted; Alberta: 'A brand-new data centre licence stands last' (first in time) — matters only if the site holds its own licence; Vancouver 2050s: snowpack in the supply watersheds 292 → 123 cm (RCP8.5, Metro Vancouver 2016) | 19 Oct 2026: Vancouver water + sewer $4.26–4.62/m³ (both on metered water); Edmonton 2026 commercial not read, placeholder $2.53–3.88/m³ from 2022–23 water and proposed 2025 wastewater and sanitary; reclaimed price not published in either region; US 20–100% of potable (grey literature)

existing_building.f: parcels with buildings whose use and age suit conversion (from the parcel tables), less what policy steers to other uses
existing_building.c: Precedents: 515 W Hastings office → Bulk Data Storage (2023); Edmonton office → data centre (2009, 2011), warehouse → data centre (Qu EDM2); Vancouver Office Conversion Policy addresses residential conversion only; no official vacancy statistics in either city; floor load: offices 2.4 kPa above the ground floor, 4.8 kPa on ground-access floors and basements (NBC 2020 / BCBC 2024 Table 4.1.5.3); computer rooms excluded from the office row; ≈ 6.0 kPa used in US VA design (claim-level transfer): upper office floors would need strengthening; both views shown, dated: UK valuation note 2017 'not readily adaptable'; 2026 note: such buildings can take another use [decision 30 Oct 2026]
existing_building.st: precedents in hand; stock at a parcel needs the parcel tables (N1–N7)

ambient_cover.f: the zone pair sets what is allowed; a louder zone is the cover — Vancouver credits no ambient noise for equipment
ambient_cover.c: Vancouver By-law 6555: quiet→quiet 55/45, activity→quiet 60/55, intermediate or activity→other 70/65 (day/night); background credited only for commercial premises. AUC Rule 012 road categories credit ambient but apply only to power plants and substations. Neither city publishes a road-noise map (traffic counts only). Edmonton Bylaw 14600 (ss. 19–22, at the property line): 50 dBA overnight next to homes, 60 next to non-residential uses; no ambient credit (bylaw14600; P-13, 30 Oct 2026)
ambient_cover.st: Vancouver in hand; Edmonton to recheck

interconnection.f: distance to the nearest interconnection point and to customers; latency targets of tens of milliseconds
interconnection.c: Why operators locate in cities: third-party (colocation) firms favour urban settings for buyer proximity (Pan Fang & Greenstein 2025); backbone networks are biased to cities that serve as interconnection points (Malecki 2002); edge latency targets of a few tens of ms, VR under 16 ms (Satyanarayanan 2017); internet exchange and customer proximity (JLARC 2024). Locations of internet exchange points in Vancouver and Edmonton not yet sourced; exchanges: Vancouver VANIX (78 participants, six connection points), UNM-Exch Canada-West (64), CSIX (16); Edmonton YEGIX (9) — operator-reported; fibre adds about 0.005 ms per km one way, small within a city; locations are not shown
interconnection.st: rationale sourced; local exchange-point locations a gap

zoning_status.f: look up the district: outright / conditional (development permit) / not listed (rezoning or text amendment)
zoning_status.c: Vancouver: "Bulk Data Storage" (s. 2) is conditional in I-2, I-1C, I-3 sub-area A and FC-2 only; not permitted elsewhere, including all commercial and mixed-use districts; CD-1 site-specific. Edmonton: no named use; the City treats large-scale data centres as Major Industrial (permitted IH; IM only where existing 1 Jan 2024); Minor Industrial permitted in BE and IM, and in IH only where it existed on 1 Jan 2024; in UI only on the NAIT Main Campus (Appendix IV, Sub-Area 2), limited to storage; in FD only as temporary outdoor storage; Direct Control site-specific; s. 7.20(3.3.2) may make an ill-fitting use discretionary ‖ 8 Nov 2026 (project decision): every Edmonton data centre is treated as Major Industrial (edm_dc_major): permitted in IH and EETC only; IM (new), BE, EETB, EETL, EETM, EETIM, EIB, EIM, FD need a rezoning. ‖ 8 Nov 2026 (mix rule): in Edmonton a data centre with public uses needs a rezoning in every zone (IH and EETC: no Community, Health or Emergency Service; BE: no Major Industrial).
zoning_status.st: sourced for standard zones; Edmonton Major or Minor turns on the data centre's own effects (Development Planner decides)

rezoning_price.f: duration + application fee + levies and charges on new floor area
rezoning_price.c: Vancouver: target ~15 months to decision (~1 year from fee to hearing); CD-1 fee $94,500 (elsewhere) or $226,300 (downtown/Broadway) + $1,590 per 100 m² under 8,000 m²; DCL industrial $112.87/m², mixed employment $211.54/m² (none if floor area does not increase); ACC $12.92–24.22/m² from 30 Sep 2026; CAC exempt for 100 % industrial after 30 Sep 2026. Also where the City attaches conditions (111 E 5th heat delivery) and residents get a say (579 submissions). Edmonton (2026 Planning and Development Fee Schedules, effective 1 Jan 2026): rezoning to an Industrial zone (BE, IM, IH, … DC/IND) $2,745 base + $340/ha; Direct Control — Administrative $7,930, Minor $7,930 + $0.62/m² buildable, Major $15,855 + $1.06/m² buildable (Major = significant change in character or intensity, comprehensive site planning with technical studies); plus a notification and engagement fee of $1,650 per component; development permit, non-residential new building $1,220 + $500 lot-grading inspection up to 500 m² GFA, + $1.20/m² above; building permit $11 per $1,000 construction value to $1 M, $10 per $1,000 above. Off-site levies (Facilities Bylaw 19340, consolidated 23 Apr 2024; Arterial Roads Bylaw 14380, consolidated May 2026) are charged as a condition of subdivision (and, for arterial roads, development permit) only within defined catchments, mostly new neighbourhoods and industrial areas; rates are set in a separate annual document (2026 Off-site Levies Approved Rates, not yet retrieved). Edmonton …
rezoning_price.st: Vancouver and Edmonton fees and durations in hand; Edmonton arterial-road assessment rates not retrieved

consultation.f: list the approvals an option needs that trigger Crown consultation, and the City commitments that apply; describe, never predict
consultation.c: BC: Water Sustainability Act licence (own water source) → Province may consult; on-site generation ≥ 50 MW or groundwater ≥ 75 L/s → EA reviewable (data centres not listed); new utility works needing a CPCN → BCUC reviews whether the Crown consulted; City land → UNDRIP Call 1.18 first right of refusal; Call 2.3 'include this in permitting decisions' (a commitment, not a legal duty); local governments have no constitutional duty to consult. Alberta: Water Act licence or public-land disposition → waits on consultation (ACO); power plant ≥ 1 MW → AUC application, Indigenous groups in the participant program only in Category A or by AUC call (Category C); a thermal plant < 10 MW on private land is Category B (not ordinarily included); Alberta's 2013 policy (amended 2020) applies to Crown decisions on provincial Crown lands and excludes access to private lands where Nations have no right of access, so a private urban site triggers it only through a Crown approval such as a water licence; no Alberta equivalent of the BC Declaration Act found
consultation.st: triggers read directly (90); whether an option meets one depends on land tenure, water source and on-site generation (60); Alberta 2013 policy read

people_affected.f: dissemination-area population × share of the DA within each radius (noise, light, heat receivers)
people_affected.c: 2021 census counts by dissemination area, spread evenly within each area onto a 100 m grid and summed within 200 m, 500 m and the sound distance: people, households, 65+, under 15, renter households, households spending 30%+ on shelter, people in low income (LIM-AT % × population). Randomly rounded; suppressed values count as 0

construction_time.f: planning and permits + construction + grid connection (often the longest)
construction_time.c: 12–18 months per building; 2–3 years to operation; grid can add 12–36 months (JLARC; IEA); Vancouver rezoning ~15 months; Edmonton permit data give build times for non-residential permits since 2024; Edmonton permit processing (targets / actual average April–June 2026): development permit, commercial or industrial new building 90 days / 73 days (76% within target); building permit, commercial/industrial 120 days / 64 days (86%); excludes notification and appeal periods
construction_time.st: in hand (transferred); local derivation possible for Edmonton

reclaimed_makeup.f: V_rec = s × make-up, with make-up = evaporation × C ÷ (C − 1)
reclaimed_makeup.c: C (cycles of concentration) 2–4 typical, up to 6 (FEMP/EPA); 4–6 run on treated municipal wastewater (US DOE-funded study, 2012; power-plant scale); s = share substituted, user-set 0–1; operator precedents 0.74–0.99 (Microsoft, operator claim); data-centre site water 0.32–0.36 L/kWh (LBNL 2024, denominator to confirm); Metro Vancouver will consider supplying reclaimed water case by case for industrial uses (UT-019, 2023); EPCOR Gold Bar already supplies treated water to industry (operator claim, no volumes); no Canadian data-centre case found
reclaimed_makeup.st: screening; Vancouver and Edmonton supply volumes and prices not found

greywater_neighbours.f: V_gw = residents within reach × 98 L/person/day × 365; used = min(V_gw × recovery, make-up)
greywater_neighbours.c: 98 L/person/day residential greywater (National Academies 2016, US data); treatment recovery share not found (gap); cross-property sharing: no BC or Alberta rule text found; San Francisco permits district-scale systems serving two or more buildings (SFPUC)

treatment_energy.c: e = 0.75–1.1 kWh/m³ greywater membrane bioreactor; 0.94–1.28 mixed wastewater (Arden et al. 2021, US EPA authors); ~4.6 kWh/m³ in one small blackwater plant (university report, low confidence); viable only where water + sewer cost ≥ US$2.38/m³ (greywater) or US$1.85/m³ (mixed) (Arden 2021, US 2020 dollars) O-19 (30 Oct 2026): arden2021 was unreachable in check 2 and its entry gives no table or page, so these figures are marked ? on screen.

blowdown_recovery.c: one US federal test (GSA GPG-052, NREL evaluation, 2023): blowdown −53 %, make-up −16 %, cycles 2.8 → 4.9; US$46.8k installed; hard water, single site (30 Oct 2026: the cycles 2.8 → 4.9 imply blowdown −54 % and make-up −19 % at constant evaporation, our arithmetic; the measured −53 % / −16 % are kept.)

pv_roof.n: Solar on the data centre roof
pv_roof.f: kWp = panel area × 0.16–0.20 kWp/m²; panel area = 12 m² × the number of 6 × 2 m panel rows that fit on the roof outside the plant and its clearances (1 m from the roof edge, an assumption; rows 0.5 m apart along, 1.5 m across); MWh = kWp × yield (horizontal to latitude tilt)
pv_roof.c: 18 Oct 2026 (sweep M102): the register now matches the layout the Solar card uses pvLayout); the earlier roof area × 0.66 × (1 − plant share) × 0.70 formula is retired. yield, annual kWh/kWp (NRCan municipal values, ±10%, losses in a 0.75 performance ratio): Vancouver 892 horizontal to 1007 at latitude tilt; Edmonton 944 to 1244. A flat-roof array at about 15° tilt lies between the two, so the tool uses horizontal as the low end and latitude tilt as the high end. Edmonton yields about 6–24% more than Vancouver per kWp. Module density 0.16 kWp/m² (2014 median) to 0.20 (current) (NREL); module cover 0.70 of a flat roof at 15° tilt; 66% of large roofs suitable (NREL 2016); roof share taken by plant from the cooling module P-05 (30 Oct 2026): 128 / 159 kWh per m² of roof is our derivation, at the optimistic end (module density × whole usable roof). Yields (30 Oct 2026, corrects P-16): NRCan published annual values everywhere: Vancouver 892 (flat) – 1,007 (latitude tilt), 716 vertical; Edmonton 944 – 1,244, 989 vertical; the monthly table sums 0–3 kWh differently from rounding.
pv_roof.pl: Solar on the data centre roof

pv_facade.f: MWh = south facade area × module density × vertical yield
pv_facade.c: vertical (south-facing, 90°) yield, annual kWh/kWp: Vancouver 716, Edmonton 989 (NRCan municipal values). Vertical gives 71% of the latitude-tilt yield in Vancouver and 80% in Edmonton; in Edmonton a south wall yields more than a flat roof (989 vs 944), because of low winter sun. Replaces the interim 0.4–0.6 factor. No Canadian BIPV cost found (30 Oct 2026: these are the NRCan published annual values, used everywhere.)

pv_share.n: Share of the data centre's power from its own solar
pv_share.c: worked check (roof areas assumed, not sourced): 1 MW IT site 1.4–4.8 %; 10 MW site 0.28–0.96 %; PV is a small share at data-centre densities; avoided carbon at the tool basis, NIR 2026 consumption intensity (2024): BC 18.1, Alberta 346.1 g CO2e/kWh (average factors)
pv_share.pl: Share of power from the building's solar

pv_cost.c: CAD 2.00–3.20/W under 100 kW; 1.90–2.40 for 100–250 kW; 1.68–2.22 above 250 kW (NRCan/IEA PVPS Canada 2024); O&M ≈ US$21/kW·yr, 30-yr life, 0.5–0.7 %/yr degradation (NREL, US)

battery.f: MWh = MW × hours (1–8, default 4); area m² = kWh ÷ 34 (19–49)
battery.c: round-trip 85% (NREL ATB 2024); PNNL 2022 LFP, 2021 US$ installed: 1 MW 518.59/kWh (2 h) and 448.34 (4 h), 10 MW 461.15 and 410.70 — about 10% above the 100 MW figure of 385; 2030: 340.46 (1 MW 4 h), 311.11 (10 MW 4 h); RTE 83% at the transformer, 2,400 cycles at 80% DOD, 16-year life; 34 ± 15 kWh/m² across built sites (Reber 2023); fire-code basis in BC/AB (NFPA 855 adoption) unconfirmed | 19 Oct 2026: cost range CAD 467–627/kWh (NREL 2025 US$334, 2024$, to PNNL 2022 1 MW 4 h US$448, 2021$; US$ × 1.3978, no inflation adjustment); O&M 2.5–4% of capex a year; 15 yr; cost per kW-year at 5.6% real compared with the programme value (Electricity card)
battery.st: in hand (1 and 10 MW costs, 16 Oct 2026); fire code a gap

genset_test.f: energy = units × kW × test hours at load; × emission factors
genset_test.c: testing ≈14.5 h/yr per unit, ~4 h at full load (AUC 27938-D01-2023, Amazon 25.6 MW, derived); Vancouver noise by-law exemption caps tests ≈15 h/yr; uncontrolled diesel 14.6 g NOx, 0.43 g PM, 706 g CO2 per kWh (AP-42 Table 3.4-1, upper bound for modern engines); Alberta exempts standby generators from environmental approval; Vancouver Noise By-law s. 4.1(c): a test is exempt from the noise limits at most once a month, daytime, up to 60 min, plus once a year up to 180 min, at no more than 80 dBA [decision 30 Oct 2026]

hvo_swap.f: Δ lifecycle CO2e = fuel energy × (CI diesel − CI renewable diesel)
hvo_swap.c: BC approved fuel codes −7 to 131 g CO2e/MJ (RLCF-012, Apr 2026); stack CO2, NOx and PM stay about the same; fossil diesel reference CI to retrieve

borefield.n: Borefield as the data centre's heat sink
borefield.f: L = heat to ground (W) ÷ q; boreholes = L ÷ 150 m; area = boreholes × 36 m²
borefield.c: q = 12 W/m (base design, 1,248 m) to 19 W/m (economic optimum, about 760 m), both for the ground-only heat-pump system; the dry-cooler hybrid only reused 760 m (derived by dividing the 14.5 kW cooling load by length, not the heat rejected to the ground, which also includes compressor work; Zurmuhl et al. 2018 s. 3.1, 4.2.1–4.2.2, a 14.5 kW data centre, Ithaca, k 3.27 W/m·K; checked 18 Oct 2026); Edmonton design k 1.9 W/m·K (Alberta Geological Survey) → ~7–11 W/m (scaling is an assumption); ≈2 ha of borefield per MW rejected; 40 MW ≈ 0.8 km²; screening only — CSA C448 sizing and a thermal response test required; no Vancouver ground data found P-22 (30 Oct 2026): "about 2 ha per MW" holds only at 12 W/m; at 19 W/m it is about 1.3 ha, and at the 7–11 W/m used for Edmonton 2.2–3.4 ha per MW (our arithmetic, same 150 m boreholes on 36 m²).
borefield.st: screening; no standard for continuous rejection
borefield.pl: Borefield as the data centre's heat sink

ground_warming.f: from the share of heat put in vs taken out
ground_warming.c: +4.7 K over 20 yr ground-only, +1.2 K with a dry cooler (Zurmuhl 2018, small field); about +3 K in 3 yr where 4.8 × more heat went in than out (Kindaichi 2018, field measurement) — a borefield only lasts if neighbours take heat back out in winter

btes.f: heat out = η × heat stored; boreholes = charge W ÷ 47–83 W/m ÷ 35–55 m
btes.c: η 0.45 steady state (simulated), 0.32–0.56 measured years 3–10, 0.06–0.21 in years 1–2 (Drake Landing, Okotoks); a 0.9 MW data-centre design: 240 boreholes, 55 m deep, 3 m apart, 1,863 m², waste-heat use 77 → 96 %, ~17-yr payback (Li et al. 2021); heat-pump COP for the lift not given (gap)
btes.st: NOT COMPUTED YET (2 Nov 2026): in hand; COP a gap

ates.f: flow (m³/h) = MW × 1,000 × 3.6 ÷ (4.18 × ΔT); heat out ≈ 0.6 × heat in
ates.c: 172 m³/h per MW at ΔT 5 K (assumption); injection ≤25 °C typical (Netherlands limit; no BC/AB limit found) — air-cooled data-centre heat (25–35 °C) may exceed it; recovery 0.6 (0.4–0.85), ≈ €300/kW at 2 MW (Barth et al. 2026); BC: water licence (WSA); Alberta: Water Act approval or licence + professional report

deep_geo.c: Edmonton: ~90 °C at 2.5 km, 30–80 kg/s → 2.1–5.6 MWth average per well pair, $4.7–8 M per well (Majorowicz & Grasby 2021); licensed by the AER (Directive 089, 2025); competes with data-centre heat as a district source rather than cooling the data centre; Vancouver: not plausible for power, direct use unproven P-21 (30 Oct 2026): the return temperature is not stated; 2.1–5.6 MWth from 30–80 kg/s implies a drop of about 16.7 K, a return near 73 °C (our arithmetic ?).

tes_volume.c: 169 L/kWh at ΔT 6 K, 34 L/kWh at 30 K (3,600 ÷ (4.18 × ΔT) ÷ 0.85; corrected 2 Nov 2026, N-22: the 0.85 had been left out); ice ≈ 10.5 kg per kWh (latent heat alone gives 3,600 ÷ 334 = 10.8 ?); usable share 0.85 and tank heights are assumptions; costs too wide to use (IRENA range)

envelope.f: max floor area = site area × FSR (or FAR) available to the data-centre use; height, setbacks and building-width limits from the zone

Hot water stored for taps must be at least 60 °C, and 49 °C anywhere in a recirculation loop (Vancouver Building By-law 2025 Book II, 2.6.1.12.(1), 2.6.1.1.(3)); so data-centre heat at 25–35 °C can preheat tap water but a heat pump or other source must finish it. Map records (15 Oct 2026, *.json): Vancouver 353 — 27 recreation centres, 1 arena, 20 hospitals, 103 care homes, 202 schools (StatCan ODRSF v2 records no separate Vancouver pools; recreation-centre contents not recorded) — plus 641 non-market housing projects (City open data); Edmonton 475 — 161 recreation centres, 23 pools, 22 indoor arenas, 13 hospitals, 2 care homes, 254 schools. 72 health records have no location and are counted, not placed. Arena ice plants are heat sources as well as receivers. | 20 Oct 2026 M87): care homes from each province's licence list replace StatCan ODHF care records. heat_plume_dT.n: Warmer air near the cooling units
heat_plume_dT.f: at the coil: ΔT = Q ÷ (ρ·cp·airflow); at a neighbour: ΔT ≈ Q ÷ (ρ·cp) × (χ/Q)(x), a plume factor (dispersion method to be chosen with the Architecture mode spatial rules; air_screen_1h was dropped 30 Oct 2026); heat treated as a passive tracer (buoyant rise ignored)
heat_plume_dT.c: airflow from manufacturer data (claim, 50); screening estimate, not a measured air temperature. Measured (first field study, Phoenix, 36–169 MW): downwind air 0.7–0.9 °C warmer on average, up to 2.2 °C, detectable 100–500 m away; condenser discharge 8–14 °C above ambient. Placement: units on the roof warm street-level air less than units on walls (Berlin model: up to 0.6 K for wall units, smaller for rooftop; Jin et al. 2020). The effect is strongest at night: Phoenix AC waste heat added more than 1 °C at night at some locations, little by day (Salamanca et al. 2014). A land-surface preprint (+2 °C) is context only

condensate.f: coils condense only when air is cooled below its dew point; hours a year with outdoor dew point above 15 °C (the top of ASHRAE's recommended IT inlet range), from CWEC
condensate.c: computed from CWEC: Vancouver 417 h, Edmonton 117 h a year with outdoor dew point above 15 °C, so little condensate from a data centre; the monthly average dew point peaks near 13 °C in Vancouver and 12 °C in Edmonton in July–August (ECCC normals, vapour pressure 1.5 and 1.4 kPa, converted); US EPA rule of thumb for offices 3–10 US gal a day per 1,000 ft² conditioned (about 0.12–0.41 L/m² a day), not for data halls; litres per kW of cooling not found (gap)

stormwater_volume.c: the lot area is used as the non-landscaped area (an upper bound); Vancouver's full engineered volume (Modified Rational Method, 2100 IDF, 10-year) is not computed; extra volume held for a neighbour or the street costs as a tank ($667–2,955 per m³, register rainwater); no dollar value of avoided sewer upgrades found in either city

snowmelt_area.n: Sidewalk kept clear by its heat
snowmelt_area.f: m² = heat offered (W) ÷ design heat per m²
snowmelt_area.c: Edmonton design 430–700 W/m² (NRC CBD 160, 1974: sheltered to very exposed); ASHRAE 2015 lists no Canadian city; Seattle, the nearest listed (27 snowfall hours a year), is used for Vancouver: 420–647 W/m² at the 99% level (snow-free area ratio 0.5 to 1), about 36 kWh/m² a year at ratio 0.5; low-temperature fluid works (Holland MI 35 °C, Klamath Falls 38 °C); snow (ECCC normals 1991–2020): Vancouver 36.6 cm a year, 7.4 days with snowfall, 8.2 days with at least 1 cm on the ground; Edmonton 126.7 cm, 54.7 days, 145.1 days; no data-centre snowmelt built (gap)

fire_water.f: a tank on the lot, non-potable, for the fire department after an earthquake; drinking water makes the operator a water supplier
fire_water.c: BCBC 2024 and NBC 3.2.5.7 (Alberta uses the NBC Alberta Edition, same clause per the NFC(AE) cross-reference): every building has water for firefighting; a sprinklered building is deemed to comply; where city supply is limited, a supply on site may be needed, sized for at least 30 minutes of fire-department hose streams (NFPA 1142 and the ISO fire flow guide named; volume not sized: standards not read). Vancouver: sprinklers rely on the mains; the seismic saltwater system (DFPS) covers downtown, part of Kitsilano and to VGH and takes about 80 years to complete. BC DWPR: a non-potable, unconnected, marked supply needs no permit; drinking water needs construction and operating permits. Alberta: drinking water piped to neighbours makes it a private utility waterworks (Potable Water Regulation s. 1(1)(l)); a registration if it only passes on city water, an approval if it draws its own source (Activities Designation Regulation); Edmonton: NBC(AE) 3.2.5.7.(1) — for buildings over 3 storeys or 600 m², municipal supply at least 3,800 L/min at 140 kPa, or an on-site volume by formula [decision 30 Oct 2026]

electrical_room.c: room: no CEC rule found that puts a UPS in a service room (CEC 26-010 covers liquid-filled equipment); NBC 2020 / VBBL 3.6.2.1.(7) require a 1 h service room for service equipment in a storey not sprinklered throughout (reading UPS and batteries as service equipment is ours ?), so the separate room is code-required only there and drawn everywhere as a choice; working space in front of the UPS 1 m (CEC 2-308), and because the Galaxy VX 1000 kW is rated 1203 A at 480 V (≥ 1200 A) the room must let a person leave without passing it, otherwise 1.5 m (CEC 2-310 2)) — the tool draws 1.5 m because doors are not placed; headroom 2.2 m at exposed live parts (2-308 5)); UPS against a wall, no rear or side access (Schneider); battery cabinets 0.914 m clear in front, 0.457 m above, 25 mm to a wall, none side to side (Vertiv, UL 9540A-tested; CEC 64-1100 9) lets UL 9540A systems follow the maker's instructions); NFPA 855 asks 0.914 m between ESS units unless fire testing shows less (adoption in BC/AB ?); corrected: a code-required electrical service room is drawn with a 1 h fire separation whether or not the storey is sprinklered (check 2; the safer reading) [decision 30 Oct 2026] [7 Nov 2026 (V339 board fixes): the Architecture drawing now draws the rooms by count to this formula: UPS frames side by side against one wall (3.6 × 0.9 m each, count from the engine with spares) + 1.5 m working space; Li-ion cabinets (0.6 × 0.75 m) 25 mm off the wall + 0.914 m in front; each …

room_cooling_type.f: hall density = heat to air on a hall floor ÷ its floor area (W/ft²); up to about 150 → room units along the walls; up to about 400 → a thermal wall in a side gallery; above → in-row coolers
room_cooling_type.c: density limits are Vertiv's claims (SL-70713): about 150 W/ft² traditional CRAH, 250 full-face, 400 thermal wall; using heat to air (not all IT heat) for liquid-cooled halls is our reading (?); thermal wall: CA80 500 kW (rating water temperatures not printed ?), 1.52 m deep × 3.96 m along the wall × 3.67 m high, side by side with a gasketed gap, 1.1 m clear on the hall and gallery sides, UL 1995; in-row: CR050RC 73.7 kW at 95 °F return, 0.6 × 1.1 m, at row ends and evenly along rows, sized with about 20% extra (Vertiv CRV catalog)

hr_flow.f: V = Q ÷ (1.16 × ΔT), at design peak (servers × capture, not the yearly average); source side (data centre → heat pump) and network side (heat pump → network) separately
hr_flow.c: network side ΔT 15 K (Vancouver NEU minimum) to 30 K (UBC operating ΔT); source side ΔT 10 K (DualPAC rating, 30 → 20 °C); Q = V × 1.16 × ΔT (heat_in_water; water 4.18 kJ/kg·K × 1,000 kg/m³ ÷ 3,600 = 1.16 kWh/m³·K, physics; a primary property table not yet cited ?)

Alberta's BYOG process for loads of 75 MW and up is a proposal (aesoBYOG2026)

Card method after the network-peak swap: peak 27-28 MW (was 16-23); base share 95 % from the UK table against the NEU's ~70 % (kept as the ceiling); capital $40-85M (NEU at the high end); cost $64-119/MWh against the NEU's $128 price (all-in, 2,000 h): middle $92 is 29 % below, high end 7 % below, low end 50 % below, so within 30 % only from the middle up. Remaining gap: cheapest pipe and best COP together at the low end, the base-share table, and the utility's return and overhead inside a price. Second check (econ_lonsdale_check): card $74-149 for an all-boiler loop brackets Lonsdale's $108 price. Superseded 13 Nov figure: $61-73 (45-55 % low)
